It turns out the advancements we’re getting in coding and computer use, combined with industry specific understand and general reasoning, can bring automation to a large number of areas of knowledge work.

We’re entering the era of autonomous collaborators in a number of industries that haven’t yet had their claude code or codex moment yet. But now this is going to happen. 

We’ll see it in animation, film production, gaming, manufacturing, architecture, product design, robotics, and more. All of these fields have the potential of driving far more output similar to what we’ve seen in software engineering. There’s no inherent finite demand for these categories of work.

“Software is eating the world” is finally in a much bigger way happening because of AI.

We’re moving from an era of AI where the output comes roughly at the rate that you can chat back and forth with the AI to work with you, to a period where you can set a problem for a set of agents to go off and do an arbitrarily large amount of work for you. This means productivity gains that are maybe 20-50% to gains that don’t really have an upper limit.

Agent swarms and the ability to fan out complex work across many agents doing tasks in parallel provide a massive unlock in a lot of spaces. This will lead to qualitatively different outcomes in my fields. 

This has already been seen across the coding domain. Next, cyber is almost entirely a problem space where more agents reviewing more things will lead to far better outcomes. We’re seeing the same now in many scientific fields, and this almost certainly will change life sciences. 

But this will increasingly be true in any field where you can parallelize computer-based work to complete something faster or do something at a totally different quality level. Which is actually are some of the most valuable domains of knowledge work today. 

Our brains aren’t really wired for the new scenario we’re heading into where compute becomes the variable that we can flex to solve any problem that we want. We’re used to thinking that the amount of time that goes into a task is correlated to the output that we get from it. And most domains of knowledge work or science have generally always been correlated with this. That’s changing forever.

Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude.

Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content.

When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

Exciting news: @AIatMeta's Muse Ember (Max) is the highest-performing small model in the Code Arena: WebDev with 1608 pts, outperforming two leading small models from Anthropic and OpenAI:
- Claude Haiku 5.5 (High): #35, 1595 pts
- GPT-6 Luna (Max): #42, 1578 pts

At a 1608 score at a median cost of $0.03 per task, this puts Ember on the Pareto frontier. Neither Haiku 5.5 nor Luna makes it. Despite all three models having the same API pricing of $0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens, Ember's median cost per task is 2× lower than Luna ($0.06) and 3.7× lower than Haiku ($0.11).

In our own testing, Ember demonstrated impressive speed and efficiency, completing 25 complex generations in 2 mins per task, at a total cost of just $1.

Huge congrats to @alexandr_wang and the @AIatMeta team on this impressive release! A major step forward for small models that deliver strong real-world coding capabilities at a fraction of the cost.

We’ve partnered with Google DeepMind to launch their Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) evaluation, a new benchmark for agentic knowledge work over complex visual files

@GoogleDeepMind’s MKA is a new benchmark requiring agents to review visually complex project files such as schematics and scans, and produce deliverables like slide decks, spreadsheets, reports, and marked-up images

Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) overview:

➤ 200 private real-world visual tasks across 10 industries: Agents work from dense visual project files including architectural drawings, engineering schematics, and clinical scans to produce deliverables including slide decks, spreadsheets, PDFs, Word documents, and marked-up images. Unlike many agentic evaluations, these inputs emphasize realistic visual complexity and domain-specificity, and are genuinely required to complete the task rather than just providing additional context

➤ Climb vs. Regression rubric scoring: Each task is graded against expert rubrics, averaging ~70 weighted criteria per task. Criteria are split into ‘Regression’ (baseline checks models should pass) and ‘Climb’ criteria (harder checks designed to separate strong models). The headline score is Climb WSR (Weighted Satisfaction Rate) - the weighted proportion Climb rubric criteria successfully completed

➤ Evaluated in Stirrup with an agentic judge: We run every task in Stirrup, our open source agent harness, with code execution, web search, web fetch, and image-viewing tools (up to 250 turns), and grade submitted deliverables using GPT-6 Luna (medium) as an agentic judge

Key MKA results:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 leads on multimodal knowledge work: Anthropic’s recently released Claude Fable 5.2 (max) leads the MKA leaderboard with a Climb WSR of 57%, followed by Gemini 4 Carbon (high) at 54% and Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 53%

➤ Cost per Task spans nearly 30× within 10 points of the top score: Claude Fable 5.2 averages $31.97 per task, over 5× Gemini 4 Carbon ($6.29) for ~2 extra points, and ~29× GPT-6.1 Sol ($1.11). Below Carbon, all four OpenAI models tested sit on the cost-performance Pareto frontier (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna), with Claude Haiku 5.5 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro making up the rest of the frontier

➤ No single model leads across all 10 industry verticals: Claude Fable 5.2 leads five verticals (Software & Data, Engineering, Logistics & Mapping, Business, and Finance alongside Claude Sonnet 5.5), Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads Education and Construction, Gemini 4 Argon (high) leads Science, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads Healthcare, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) narrowly leads Law & Government

Thank you to the @GoogleDeepMind team for their work building this benchmark and collaborating with us to bring it exclusively to Artificial Analysis!

Keenable Search 1.0 takes 1st (pro, 83) and 2nd (realtime, 82) on the Artificial Analysis Search Index: ahead of Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Perplexity (medium) at 80

We benchmarked both modes of @KeenableAI's Keenable Search 1.0, pro and realtime, in our Stirrup agent harness with Keenable Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

At $4 per 1k searches, Keenable costs about $0.040 per task in both modes, over a third below the board median ($0.063). It is also one of the fastest products we measure: 15.0s (realtime) and 15.5s (pro) per task, 2nd and 3rd on the board.

Key benchmarking results for Keenable Search 1.0:

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: Keenable (pro) scores 83 and Keenable (realtime) 82, up from 67 for both modes when we first benchmarked Keenable in August, and a ~50-point lift over the same model with no search (33). Both lead Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Perplexity (medium) at 80

➤ DeepSearchQA is Keenable's strongest benchmark: both modes score 88 F1, 1st and 2nd of 26, ahead of Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) at 86. Pro also ranks 1st on BrowseComp (87%, level with Perplexity (medium)) and on AA-Omniscience (73%, level with Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Firecrawl)

➤ Fast search: realtime takes 2.3s of search time per task (2nd of 26) and pro 3.0s (3rd), against a board median of 12.5s. Each search returns in about 330ms (realtime) and 390ms (pro) on average

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Keenable Search API with mode=realtime and mode=pro

➤ Pricing: $4 per 1k requests in both modes (public pay-as-you-go price)

➤ Cards: We disabled Keenable's search cards for testing (disable_cards=true)
Great to partner with @GoogleDeepMind in bringing MKA Benchmark to Artificial Analysis

A few tips for getting the most out of it:
- Ask what’s wrong with your idea before it builds anything. It’s great at brainstorming and will push back
- Start on med/high effort, and save xhigh for hardest problems
- Tell it up front what needs your approval (e.g. deleting things) and that the rest is its call
- Give it a whole project instead of a next step and let it run for hours. This is where it shines

At @vercel we got to test this model before release. Best way to summarize it: astonishingly brilliant.

One interesting takeaway: it's very clear that this new generation of models can take on unprecedented bodies of parallel work.

To actually seize this intelligence, you need cloud sandboxes. Full stop. The model can delegate and orchestrate far more than a single computer can handle. Likely far more than you can even imagine it can handle.

Your bottleneck is now ① your ambition and ② your parallel computing power.

Btw, I learned from @cramforce you don't need to overcomplicate it. Install Vercel CLI, setup the Plugin and tell the agent to use /𝚘𝚏𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚊𝚍-𝚝𝚘-𝚜𝚊𝚗𝚍𝚋𝚘𝚡 skill. It'll provision and de-allocate cloud sandboxes as needed. You don't need a "multi-agent remote harness ralph orchestrator" 😆

So bullish on MCP. Its utility exceeds the "M" part: even AI aside, it'll be a civilization-scale accomplishment to get all our systems communicating through one universal open protocol.

A missing piece was how to get arbitrary callbacks across sessions. MCP could read and write, but it couldn't tell you later "this event happened." MCP Events fixes this.

We're adding support in our own MCP. Say an agent makes a deployment, and wants to know when it's complete. Instead of polling, it can subscribe to 𝚍𝚎𝚙𝚕𝚘𝚢𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝.𝚜𝚞𝚌𝚌𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚎𝚍.

PSA: With Vercel Queues and Workflows, writing the backend machinery for your own MCPs to do this is easy peasy.

Very few things in nature are true long-term exponentials. Most follow S-curves.

I saw this when I worked at Facebook. What looked like clean exponential growth was actually a series of overlapping S-curves, each driven by technological breakthroughs and/or adoption waves.

AI is probably the same. That doesn’t mean progress will have to slow down, but sustained exponential growth isn’t automatic either.
